<!--
PURPOSE   Explains the 12-month recession-probability model used by the
          TerraMetric Atlas growth-outlook card: the data it reads, the maths
          of each step, how it is validated, and where it can mislead.
          The model code lives in R/synopsis_tier3.R (section "RECESSION
          MODEL"); this document does not re-implement it, it reads a
          snapshot produced by running that code.
PARAMS    snapshot_path  path to the snapshot RDS (default below).
BUILD     1. From the repo root (needs FRED_API_KEY, see .Renviron.example):
               Rscript docs/build_recession_snapshot.R      (~90 s)
          2. quarto render docs/recession_model.qmd
DEPENDS   R: glmnet, zoo, lubridate, fredr (snapshot) and dplyr, tidyr,
          ggplot2, scales, gt, htmltools, knitr (this document).
          Quarto >= 1.4. No network needed at render time.
-->

```{r}
#| label: params
#| tags: [parameters]
#| include: false
snapshot_path <- "recession_model_snapshot.rds"
```

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(ggplot2)
  library(scales); library(gt); library(htmltools); library(lubridate)
})

# ── Brand palette ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
NAVY <- "#1B2A4A"; ORANGE <- "#FC6600"; TEAL <- "#2EC4B6"
GREY <- "#6c757d"; GREEN <- "#198754"; RED <- "#dc3545"; AMBER <- "#d97706"

theme_atlas <- function(base_size = 12) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size, base_family = "sans") +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(color = NAVY, face = "bold"),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(color = GREY),
      axis.title = element_text(color = NAVY),
      axis.text = element_text(color = NAVY),
      axis.line.x = element_line(color = "#ced4da"),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#e9ecef"),
      strip.text = element_text(color = NAVY, face = "bold"),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA)
    )
}
theme_set(theme_atlas())

# ── Formatting helpers ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fmt_pct <- function(x, d = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), 100 * x)
fmt_pp  <- function(x, d = 1) sprintf(paste0("%+.", d, " pp"), 100 * x)
fmt_mon <- function(x) format(x, "%b %Y")

# ── HTML helpers (return a string; call inside cat() in an `output: asis` chunk)
kpi_card <- function(label, value, sub = "", color = NAVY) {
  sprintf(
    '<div style="flex:1 1 170px;border-left:5px solid %s;background:%s14;padding:.65rem .9rem;border-radius:4px;">
       <div style="font-size:.72rem;letter-spacing:.04em;text-transform:uppercase;color:%s;">%s</div>
       <div style="font-size:1.7rem;font-weight:700;color:%s;line-height:1.15;">%s</div>
       <div style="font-size:.78rem;color:%s;">%s</div></div>',
    color, color, GREY, label, color, value, GREY, sub
  )
}
raw_html <- function(x) {
  fence <- strrep("`", 3)
  paste0("\n", fence, "{=html}\n", x, "\n", fence, "\n")
}
kpi_row <- function(...) {
  raw_html(paste0('<div style="display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:12px;margin:1rem 0;">',
                  paste0(c(...), collapse = ""), "</div>"))
}
callout <- function(kind, title, body) {
  col <- c(inputs = TEAL, logic = NAVY, output = GREEN, warn = AMBER, note = GREY)[[kind]]
  raw_html(sprintf(
    '<div style="border-left:4px solid %s;background:%s1a;padding:.7rem 1rem;margin:1rem 0;border-radius:4px;">
       <div style="font-weight:700;color:%s;margin-bottom:.2rem;">%s</div><div>%s</div></div>',
    col, col, col, title, body
  ))
}
formula_box <- function(text, caption = "") {
  raw_html(sprintf(
    '<div style="margin:1rem 0;"><pre style="background:#f1f3f5;color:%s;border:1px solid #dee2e6;border-radius:4px;padding:.8rem 1rem;overflow-x:auto;font-size:.82rem;">%s</pre>
     <div style="font-size:.78rem;color:%s;margin-top:-.4rem;">%s</div></div>',
    NAVY, text, GREY, caption
  ))
}
gt_atlas <- function(g) {
  g |>
    tab_options(
      table.font.size = px(13), data_row.padding = px(4),
      column_labels.background.color = "#f1f3f5",
      column_labels.font.weight = "bold",
      table.width = pct(100)
    )
}

# ── Snapshot ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
snap   <- readRDS(snapshot_path)
K      <- snap$consts
P      <- K$predictors
m      <- snap$live$model
cur    <- snap$current
bt     <- snap$live$backtest
fc     <- cur$factor_contributions
panel  <- snap$panel
train  <- snap$train
latest <- snap$latest
jan_asof <- as.Date(format(latest, "%Y-01-01"))

eta     <- m$intercept + sum(fc$contribution)
cvfit   <- m$fit
i1se    <- which(cvfit$lambda == cvfit$lambda.1se)
imin    <- which(cvfit$lambda == cvfit$lambda.min)
null_dev <- -2 * (m$base_rate * log(m$base_rate) + (1 - m$base_rate) * log(1 - m$base_rate))
sum_abs_beta <- sum(abs(m$beta))
p_max <- plogis(m$intercept + 3 * sum_abs_beta)

# NBER recession spells for chart shading
rle_r <- rle(panel$recession == 1)
ends_i <- cumsum(rle_r$lengths); starts_i <- ends_i - rle_r$lengths + 1
nber <- data.frame(xmin = panel$date[starts_i[rle_r$values]],
                   xmax = panel$date[ends_i[rle_r$values]])
shade_nber <- function(from = min(panel$date)) {
  geom_rect(data = nber[nber$xmax >= from, ], inherit.aes = FALSE,
            aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
            fill = GREY, alpha = 0.18)
}
```

# 1 — Summary

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
tier_col <- c(Low = GREEN, "Low–Moderate" = AMBER, Moderate = AMBER, High = RED, Elevated = RED)[[cur$tier$label]]
cat(kpi_row(
  kpi_card("12-month recession probability", fmt_pct(snap$live$prob), paste("as of", fmt_mon(cur$month)), tier_col),
  kpi_card("Tier", cur$tier$label, "5-tier scale, section 6.4", tier_col),
  kpi_card("Training window", paste(m$n_train, "months"), paste(fmt_mon(min(train$date)), "–", fmt_mon(m$train_end)), NAVY),
  kpi_card("Backtest skill vs climatology", sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * bt$skill), sprintf("Brier %.3f vs %.3f", bt$brier, bt$brier_clim), TEAL),
  kpi_card("Backtest AUC", sprintf("%.2f", bt$auc), sprintf("%d scored months, %s–", bt$n, format(bt$from, "%Y")), TEAL)
))
```

The model answers one question: **what is the probability that the NBER will date at least one month of recession in the next 12 months?** The answer is a number between 0 and 1, recomputed daily from public FRED data.

- It is a **logistic regression** on nine macro indicators (yield curve, labor, credit, sentiment, policy stance).
- The coefficients are fitted by **Ridge regularisation** (shrinks them toward zero) and **sign-constrained** (each one may only push risk in the direction macro theory expects).
- It is **refit every January** on the latest 360 months (30 years) whose outcome is already known.
- It is validated with a **walk-forward backtest** from 1985 that repeats the same January refit using only information available at the time.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A["FRED<br/>13 monthly series"] --> B["Monthly panel<br/>9 predictors + NBER label"]
  B --> C["Training rows<br/>latest 360 labelled months,<br/>12-month embargo"]
  C --> D["Robust scaler<br/>median / MAD, clamp ±3"]
  D --> E["Ridge logit<br/>glmnet, sign-constrained,<br/>λ from 5-fold CV"]
  E --> F["p = σ(β₀ + Σ βⱼ zⱼ)"]
  B --> F
  F --> G["Growth-outlook card,<br/>GDP drag, LLM context"]
```

# 2 — Data

## 2.1 Source series

All inputs come from the St. Louis Fed's FRED API (`fredr`), pulled at monthly frequency from January 1959. FRED's monthly conversion of daily and weekly series is a **simple average** over the month. The app re-fetches once a day, because FRED adds a month at a time and revises recent values.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-series
src <- data.frame(
  id = K$series,
  description = c(
    "NBER recession indicator (1 = month between a peak and its trough)",
    "10-year minus 2-year Treasury constant-maturity spread (daily)",
    "10-year Treasury yield (daily); backup for the spread",
    "2-year Treasury yield (daily); backup for the spread",
    "Unemployment rate, U-3 (SA)",
    "Total unemployed + marginally attached + part-time for economic reasons, U-6 (SA)",
    "Total nonfarm payrolls, thousands (SA)",
    "Effective federal funds rate (monthly average)",
    "CPI-U, all items (SA)",
    "labor-force participation rate, ages 25–54 (SA)",
    "University of Michigan consumer sentiment index (monthly from 1978, quarterly before)",
    "Moody's Baa corporate yield minus the 10-year Treasury yield",
    "Initial jobless claims (weekly, SA)"
  ),
  feeds = c(
    "target label", "yield_spread", "yield_spread (backup)", "yield_spread (backup)",
    "u_rise, gap_rise", "gap_rise", "pay_3m", "real_rate", "real_rate",
    "prime_lfpr", "sent_chg12", "baa_spread", "claims_rise"
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
src |>
  left_join(snap$series_meta, by = "id") |>
  transmute(
    Series = id, Description = description, `Feeds` = feeds,
    `First obs` = fmt_mon(first), `Last obs` = fmt_mon(last),
    Observations = n_obs, `Gap-filled` = n_filled
  ) |>
  gt() |> gt_atlas() |>
  cols_align("right", columns = c(Observations, `Gap-filled`)) |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(font = "monospace", weight = "bold"), locations = cells_body(Series))
```

## 2.2 Cleaning and the monthly panel

### Inputs

The thirteen monthly series above, each on its own native start date.

### How it is applied

1. **Common calendar.** Every series is matched onto the contiguous monthly grid of `USREC`. A lag is always a *calendar* lag (`t − 12 months`), never a row offset, so a missing month cannot silently shift a feature.
2. **Single-month gap filling.** An `NA` is filled only if **both** neighbouring months are present. For a strictly positive series the fill is the geometric mean, otherwise the arithmetic mean:

$$
\hat v_t \;=\; \begin{cases}\sqrt{v_{t-1}\,v_{t+1}} & \text{if } v>0 \text{ throughout}\\[2pt] \tfrac12\,(v_{t-1}+v_{t+1}) & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
$$

   Longer gaps stay missing. `USREC`, `T10Y2Y`, `DGS10`, `DGS2` and `BAA10YM` are never filled (an indicator or a rate is not interpolated).
3. **Completeness rule.** A month is usable (`complete`) only when all nine predictors exist. One exception: `gap_rise` (needs U-6, which starts in 1994) may be missing *before its first observation*, where it is scored as the training median ($z=0$). After 1994 a missing value blocks the month.

### What it produces

A table of `r nrow(panel)` monthly rows (`r fmt_mon(min(panel$date))` – `r fmt_mon(max(panel$date))`) of which `r sum(panel$complete)` are `complete`, the first being `r fmt_mon(min(panel$date[panel$complete]))`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-availability
#| fig-cap: "Coverage of each source series. The model's usable history starts where the last predictor arrives; the training window sits well inside it."
av <- snap$series_meta |>
  mutate(id = factor(id, levels = rev(id)))
ggplot(av, aes(y = id)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = first, xend = last, yend = id), color = TEAL, linewidth = 4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = min(train$date), linetype = 2, color = ORANGE) +
  annotate("text", x = min(train$date), y = 0.4, label = "  current training window starts",
           hjust = 0, color = ORANGE, size = 3.5) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(callout("note", "Pre-1978 sentiment is sparse",
  "UMCSENT is only monthly from 1978; before that it is quarterly, so earlier panel rows are complete only in quarter-end months. This matters for the first walk-forward fits (1985–1990), which train on a short, sparse history, but not for the current window (1995–)."))
```

## 2.3 The nine predictors

Each predictor is a transformation of the series above chosen to carry a *leading* signal rather than a level that merely tracks the cycle. Notation: $U$ unemployment (U-3), $G=\text{U6}-\text{U3}$, $\min_{12}(x)_t=\min(x_{t-11},\dots,x_t)$ the trailing 12-month low (current month included).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-predictors
pred_tbl <- data.frame(
  predictor = P,
  definition = c(
    "T10Y2Yₜ  (backup: DGS10 − DGS2)",
    "Uₜ − min₁₂(U)ₜ",
    "Gₜ − min₁₂(G)ₜ",
    "mean of the last 3 monthly changes in PAYEMS",
    "FEDFUNDSₜ − 100·(CPIₜ / CPIₜ₋₁₂ − 1)",
    "LNS11300060ₜ (level)",
    "UMCSENTₜ − UMCSENTₜ₋₁₂",
    "BAA10YMₜ",
    "100·(ICSAₜ / min₁₂(ICSA)ₜ − 1)"
  ),
  unit = c("pp", "pp", "pp", "000 jobs / mo", "pp", "%", "index pts", "pp", "%"),
  why = c(
    "Inversion has preceded every post-war recession; a steeper curve means easier expected policy.",
    "How far unemployment has risen off its 12-month low (a Sahm-rule style trigger, on the raw monthly rate rather than a 3-month average).",
    "Involuntary part-time and marginally attached workers rise before headline unemployment does.",
    "Hiring momentum; smooths single-month payroll noise.",
    "Ex-post real policy rate: tight policy is a headwind with a lag.",
    "Slack in the core working-age population that the unemployment rate hides.",
    "Falling household confidence leads spending.",
    "Credit stress: investors demand more to hold corporate risk.",
    "Layoffs picking up from a cyclical low."
  ),
  sign = K$sign[P],
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
first_av <- vapply(P, function(v) fmt_mon(min(panel$date[!is.na(panel[[v]])])), "")
pred_tbl |>
  mutate(
    `Expected sign` = ifelse(sign > 0, "+ (higher → more risk)", "− (higher → less risk)"),
    `First value` = first_av[predictor]
  ) |>
  transmute(Predictor = predictor, Definition = definition, Unit = unit,
            `Expected sign`, `First value`, Rationale = why) |>
  gt() |> gt_atlas() |>
  tab_style(cell_text(font = "monospace", weight = "bold"), cells_body(Predictor))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(callout("warn", "Definitions worth knowing",
  paste0("<b>real_rate</b> uses trailing CPI inflation, not expected inflation, so it is an ex-post measure. ",
         "<b>u_rise</b> is called the Sahm rule in the app, but the classical Sahm rule uses the 3-month average of unemployment; this model uses the raw monthly rate, which is noisier. ",
         "<b>claims_rise</b> and the rate series are averaged to monthly from weekly or daily data.")))
```

# 3 — Target and training window

### Inputs

The `USREC` series and the nine predictors.

### How it is applied

**Target.** For month $t$, with $R_s=1$ if month $s$ lies in an NBER recession:

$$
y_t \;=\; \mathbf 1\!\Big[\,\exists\,k\in\{1,\dots,12\}:\; R_{t+k}=1\Big].
$$

So $y_t=1$ means "a recession month occurs somewhere in the next 12 months", and **a month already in recession can still score 0** if the recession ends within the year. $y_t$ is undefined (`NA`) when fewer than six future months are observed.

**Training rows.** A model fitted "as of" date $a$ uses only rows that are (i) `complete`, (ii) have a defined $y_t$, and (iii) satisfy $t\le a-12$ months — the **12-month embargo**, because $y_t$ is only fully known 12 months later. Of those it keeps the **latest 360**.

**Refit schedule.** The live model is fitted as of **January 1 of the latest scored year**. The walk-forward backtest uses the identical rule for every year.

### What it produces

For the current model (as of `r fmt_mon(jan_asof)`): `r nrow(train)` training rows from `r fmt_mon(min(train$date))` to `r fmt_mon(max(train$date))`, of which `r sum(train$rec_next12)` have $y=1$ — a **training base rate of `r fmt_pct(m$base_rate)`**.

```{r}
#| label: fig-window
#| fig-height: 2.2
#| fig-cap: "Timeline of the live model. Labels in the embargo are not yet resolved, so the model never trains on the most recent 12 months; it scores every month of the current year."
a <- jan_asof
seg <- data.frame(
  part = factor(c("Earlier history (not used)", "Training window (360 labelled months)",
                  "Embargo (labels unresolved)", "Scored by this model"),
                levels = c("Earlier history (not used)", "Training window (360 labelled months)",
                           "Embargo (labels unresolved)", "Scored by this model")),
  xmin = c(min(panel$date[panel$complete]), min(train$date), m$train_end %m+% months(1), a),
  xmax = c(min(train$date) %m-% months(1), m$train_end, a %m-% months(1), latest)
)
ggplot(seg) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = 0, ymax = 1, fill = part), color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#ced4da", NAVY, AMBER, ORANGE), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "5 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-target
#| fig-cap: "NBER recession months (grey) and the target y: 1 in the 12 months before and during each recession, 0 otherwise."
tg <- panel[!is.na(panel$rec_next12), ]
ggplot(tg, aes(date, rec_next12)) +
  shade_nber() +
  geom_area(fill = ORANGE, alpha = 0.55) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "y = recession in next 12 months")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(callout("warn", "The most recent labels are right-censored",
  "FRED's USREC is 0 until the NBER announces a peak, and that announcement typically lags by months and sometimes by more than a year. A recession that began recently would still read 0. The 12-month embargo protects the <i>training</i> set against most of this, but the final months of the backtest (where only 6–11 future months are observed) can count a pending recession as a 0."))
```

# 4 — Preprocessing: the robust scaler

### Inputs

The nine predictors for the training rows only.

### How it is applied

Each predictor has a center and scale estimated **on the training rows**, then every row (training and scoring) is transformed:

$$
z_{tj} \;=\; \operatorname{clamp}_{[-3,\,3]}\!\left(\frac{x_{tj}-\operatorname{med}_j}{\operatorname{MAD}_j}\right),
\qquad
\operatorname{MAD}_j = 1.4826\cdot\operatorname{median}\big|x_{ij}-\operatorname{med}_j\big| .
$$

- **Median/MAD instead of mean/SD**, so a few extreme months (2008, 2020) do not stretch the scale. The 1.4826 factor makes MAD comparable to a standard deviation for a normal variable.
- **Clamping at ±3** stops any single extreme reading from dominating the score.
- A missing value becomes $z=0$ (the training median): neutral.
- The scaler is built **only from training rows**, so a scoring month never influences its own scale (no look-ahead).

### What it produces

The center and scale below and today's standardised readings. A $z$ of 1 means "one robust standard deviation above the 30-year median".

```{r}
#| label: tbl-scaler
data.frame(
  Predictor = P,
  Median = m$scaler$center[P], MAD = m$scaler$scale[P],
  Raw = fc$raw_value[match(unname(K$labels[P]), fc$name)],
  z = fc$z_score[match(unname(K$labels[P]), fc$name)]
) |>
  gt() |> gt_atlas() |>
  fmt_number(c(Median, MAD, Raw, z), decimals = 2) |>
  tab_spanner("Training window", c(Median, MAD)) |>
  tab_spanner(paste("Latest month,", fmt_mon(cur$month)), c(Raw, z)) |>
  tab_style(cell_text(font = "monospace", weight = "bold"), cells_body(Predictor))
```

# 5 — Estimation: sign-constrained Ridge logistic regression

### Inputs

The scaled matrix $Z\in\mathbb R^{360\times 9}$ and the labels $y\in\{0,1\}^{360}$.

### How it is applied

**Model.** The log-odds ("logit") is linear in the standardised predictors:

$$
\eta_t=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^{9}\beta_j z_{tj},\qquad
\Pr(y_t=1\mid z_t)=\sigma(\eta_t)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\eta_t}} .
$$

**Estimation.** `glmnet` with $\alpha=0$ (pure Ridge) minimises the penalised negative log-likelihood, subject to box constraints on every slope:

$$
\min_{\beta_0,\boldsymbol\beta}\;
-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Big[y_i\,\eta_i-\log\!\big(1+e^{\eta_i}\big)\Big]
\;+\;\frac{\lambda}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{9}\tilde\beta_j^{\,2}
\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad
\ell_j\le\beta_j\le u_j .
$$

- $\tilde\beta_j=\beta_j\,\operatorname{sd}(z_j)$ is the coefficient on a unit-variance column: `glmnet` standardises internally (its default), so the penalty treats every predictor equally. The reported $\beta_j$ are on the $z$ scale.
- The **intercept is not penalised**.
- **Ridge** shrinks all coefficients toward zero smoothly and, unlike Lasso, keeps correlated predictors (yield spread, credit spread, claims) together instead of picking one. Equivalent view: a Gaussian prior on each standardised slope with standard deviation $1/\sqrt{N\lambda}$ — here $\approx$ `r sprintf("%.2f", 1 / sqrt(m$n_train * cvfit$lambda.1se))`.
- **Sign constraints.** Each predictor has a theory-based expected sign $s_j$ (table in section 2.3). Positive: $[\ell_j,u_j]=[0,\infty)$; negative: $(-\infty,0]$. A coefficient is allowed to be exactly 0 but never to flip sign. This removes late-cycle artefacts such as "tighter policy → *less* risk" that an unconstrained fit finds in some windows.

**Choosing the penalty $\lambda$.** `cv.glmnet` evaluates a path of `r length(cvfit$lambda)` values of $\lambda$ (here `r sprintf("%.3f", min(cvfit$lambda))` to `r sprintf("%.0f", max(cvfit$lambda))`) with **5-fold cross-validation** scored by binomial deviance, $D=-2\,\overline{\,y\log\hat p+(1-y)\log(1-\hat p)\,}$:

$$
\lambda_{\min}=\arg\min_\lambda \overline{D}(\lambda),\qquad
\lambda_{1\mathrm{se}}=\max\Big\{\lambda:\ \overline{D}(\lambda)\le \overline{D}(\lambda_{\min})+\operatorname{SE}\big(\overline D(\lambda_{\min})\big)\Big\}.
$$

The model uses **$\lambda_{1\mathrm{se}}$**: the most heavily penalised model that is statistically indistinguishable from the best. It deliberately trades a little in-sample fit for stability. The folds are **fixed and class-stratified** (seed `20260101`) so that identical data always give an identical $\lambda$; the default random folds moved $\lambda_{1\mathrm{se}}$ enough to swing the headline probability between restarts. Contiguous time-block folds were tried and rejected: with rare recessions a block can leave a training split with no positives.

### What it produces

The fitted intercept and nine slopes, and the chosen penalty.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cv
#| fig-cap: "Left: 5-fold CV deviance across the penalty path (dashed lines: λ_min and the chosen λ_1se; the dotted line is the deviance of a constant-base-rate model). Right: coefficient paths; every slope is held on its theory side of zero."
cvd <- data.frame(loglam = log(cvfit$lambda), cvm = cvfit$cvm, lo = cvfit$cvm - cvfit$cvsd, hi = cvfit$cvm + cvfit$cvsd)
p1 <- ggplot(cvd, aes(loglam, cvm)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = TEAL, alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(color = NAVY, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = null_dev, linetype = 3, color = GREY) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = log(c(cvfit$lambda.min, cvfit$lambda.1se)), linetype = 2, color = ORANGE) +
  annotate("text", x = log(cvfit$lambda.1se), y = max(cvd$cvm), label = " λ_1se", hjust = 0, color = ORANGE) +
  labs(x = "log λ", y = "CV binomial deviance")
bm <- as.matrix(cvfit$glmnet.fit$beta)
path <- data.frame(loglam = rep(log(cvfit$glmnet.fit$lambda), each = nrow(bm)),
                   term = rep(rownames(bm), times = ncol(bm)), beta = as.vector(bm))
p2 <- ggplot(path, aes(loglam, beta, color = term)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = log(cvfit$lambda.1se), linetype = 2, color = ORANGE) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(log(cvfit$lambda.min) - 0.2, log(cvfit$lambda.1se) + 3)) +
  labs(x = "log λ", y = "β (on the z scale)", color = NULL) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 3))
if (requireNamespace("patchwork", quietly = TRUE)) {
  patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2, nrow = 1)
} else { print(p1); print(p2) }
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-betas
bt_tbl <- data.frame(
  Predictor = P, Label = unname(K$labels[P]),
  Sign = ifelse(K$sign[P] > 0, "+", "−"),
  beta = m$beta[P]
) |> mutate(`Odds ratio per +1 z` = exp(beta),
            Status = ifelse(beta == 0, "constraint binding / shrunk to 0", "active"))
bind_rows(
  data.frame(Predictor = "(intercept)", Label = "Baseline log-odds", Sign = "", beta = m$intercept,
             `Odds ratio per +1 z` = NA_real_, Status = "unpenalised", check.names = FALSE),
  bt_tbl
) |>
  gt() |> gt_atlas() |>
  fmt_number(c(beta, `Odds ratio per +1 z`), decimals = 3) |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "") |>
  cols_label(beta = "β") |>
  tab_style(cell_text(font = "monospace", weight = "bold"), cells_body(Predictor))
```

On the training window the cross-validated deviance at $\lambda_{1\mathrm{se}}$ is `r sprintf("%.3f", cvfit$cvm[i1se])` versus `r sprintf("%.3f", null_dev)` for a model that only knows the base rate — a **`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (1 - cvfit$cvm[i1se] / null_dev))` reduction**. The standard error of the minimum is `r sprintf("%.3f", cvfit$cvsd[imin])`. Note the chosen $\lambda$ is `r sprintf("%.1f", cvfit$lambda.1se / cvfit$lambda.min)`× the CV-minimising one.

# 6 — Scoring and explaining the current reading

## 6.1 The calculation

### Inputs

The latest month's nine raw values, the fitted $\beta$ and the training scaler.

### How it is applied

1. Standardise: $z_j=\operatorname{clamp}\big((x_j-\operatorname{med}_j)/\operatorname{MAD}_j\big)$.
2. Each predictor's **log-odds contribution** is $c_j=\beta_j z_j$.
3. Sum and squash: $\eta=\beta_0+\sum_j c_j$, $p=\sigma(\eta)$.

### What it produces

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
fcs <- fc[order(-abs(fc$contribution)), ]
lines <- sprintf("%-46s beta %+6.3f  x  z %+6.2f  =  %+7.3f", fcs$name, fcs$beta, fcs$z_score, fcs$contribution)
txt <- paste0(
  paste(lines, collapse = "\n"),
  sprintf("\n%s\n%-46s %29s %+7.3f", strrep("-", 88), "Sum of contributions", "", sum(fc$contribution)),
  sprintf("\n%-46s %29s %+7.3f", "Intercept (beta0)", "", m$intercept),
  sprintf("\n%-46s %29s %+7.3f", "Log-odds  eta", "", eta),
  sprintf("\n%-46s %29s %7.1f%%", "p = 1 / (1 + exp(-eta))", "", 100 * plogis(eta))
)
cat(formula_box(txt, paste("Worked example for", fmt_mon(cur$month), "- the app displays", sprintf("%.1f%%", cur$prob))))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-contrib
#| fig-cap: "β·z contribution of each predictor to today's log-odds. Bars to the right raise recession risk; bars to the left lower it. The intercept sets the baseline risk before any information."
fc |>
  mutate(name = factor(name, levels = rev(name[order(-abs(contribution))])),
         dir = ifelse(contribution > 0, "raises risk", "lowers risk")) |>
  ggplot(aes(contribution, name, fill = dir)) +
  geom_col() + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = NAVY) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("raises risk" = RED, "lowers risk" = GREEN), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "log-odds contribution (β × z)", y = NULL)
```

## 6.2 Reading a coefficient

The slopes are on the standardised scale, so they are directly comparable: $e^{\beta_j}$ is the **multiplicative change in the odds** of a recession when predictor $j$ rises by one robust standard deviation, other things equal. Because of the logistic curve, the effect on the *probability* depends on where you start. At today's reading ($p=$ `r fmt_pct(plogis(eta))`):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens
sens <- data.frame(
  Predictor = P,
  `z rises by 1` = plogis(eta + m$beta[P]) - plogis(eta),
  `z falls by 1` = plogis(eta - m$beta[P]) - plogis(eta),
  check.names = FALSE
)
sens |>
  gt() |> gt_atlas() |>
  fmt_percent(c(`z rises by 1`, `z falls by 1`), decimals = 1, force_sign = TRUE) |>
  tab_spanner("Change in probability (percentage points of p)", c(`z rises by 1`, `z falls by 1`)) |>
  tab_style(cell_text(font = "monospace", weight = "bold"), cells_body(Predictor))
```

## 6.3 What the model cannot say

Because each $z$ is clamped to $\pm3$ and $\beta$ is shrunk, the output is bounded. With the current coefficients ($\sum_j|\beta_j|=$ `r sprintf("%.2f", sum_abs_beta)`) the highest probability the model can ever produce is `r fmt_pct(p_max)` and the lowest is `r fmt_pct(plogis(m$intercept - 3 * sum_abs_beta), 3)`. The model is therefore never "certain", which is appropriate for an indicator built from a handful of historical recessions.

## 6.4 Tiers

The app reports the probability in one of five labelled tiers (function `.classify_recession_tier`):

| Probability | Tier | color |
|---|---|---|
| $<15\%$ | Low | green |
| $15$–$30\%$ | Low–Moderate | amber |
| $30$–$50\%$ | Moderate | amber |
| $50$–$65\%$ | High | red-orange |
| $\ge 65\%$ | Elevated | red |

# 7 — Validation

### Inputs

The full panel (1976–), the same fitting code as the live model.

### How it is applied

**Walk-forward backtest.** For every year $Y$ from 1985, fit the model *as of 1 January $Y$* — using only labels that had resolved by then — and score each complete month of year $Y$. Each month's probability is therefore pseudo-out-of-sample: it never uses a label that was unknown at the time.

**Metrics** (over months whose $y$ is defined; $\hat p$ is the backtest probability):

$$
\text{Brier}=\overline{(\hat p-y)^2},\qquad
\text{Skill}=1-\frac{\text{Brier}}{\text{Brier}_{\text{clim}}},
$$

where $\text{Brier}_{\text{clim}}$ scores each month with its own training base rate. **AUC** is the probability that a randomly chosen pre-recession month ($y=1$) gets a higher $\hat p$ than a randomly chosen calm month ($y=0$), computed from ranks (Mann–Whitney). **Hit rate** is $\Pr(\hat p>0.5\mid y=1)$ and **false-alarm rate** $\Pr(\hat p>0.5\mid y=0)$.

### What it produces

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(kpi_row(
  kpi_card("Brier score", sprintf("%.3f", bt$brier), sprintf("climatology %.3f", bt$brier_clim), NAVY),
  kpi_card("Skill vs climatology", sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * bt$skill), "1 − Brier / Brier_clim", TEAL),
  kpi_card("AUC", sprintf("%.3f", bt$auc), "ranking ability", TEAL),
  kpi_card("Hit rate at 50%", fmt_pct(bt$hit_rate, 0), "months before/in recession flagged", AMBER),
  kpi_card("False-alarm rate at 50%", fmt_pct(bt$false_alarm_rate), "calm months flagged", GREEN)
))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-backtest
#| fig-cap: "Walk-forward probability since 1985 (grey bands: NBER recessions). The dashed lines are the tier cut-offs at 15%, 30%, 50% and 65%."
bs <- bt$series
ggplot(bs, aes(date, prob)) +
  shade_nber(min(bs$date)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(.15, .30, .50, .65), linetype = 2, color = "#adb5bd") +
  geom_line(color = NAVY, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = bs[nrow(bs), ], color = ORANGE, size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "P(recession in next 12 months)")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-episodes
bt$episodes |>
  transmute(Recession = recession, `Peak in the 12 months before it began` = runup_peak,
            `Peak while the y = 1 spell lasted` = spell_peak) |>
  gt() |> gt_atlas() |>
  fmt_percent(c(2, 3), decimals = 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-calibration
#| tbl-cap: "Calibration: within each probability band, how often a recession actually followed."
d <- bs[!is.na(bs$rec_next12), ]
d$band <- cut(d$prob, c(0, .15, .30, .50, .65, 1), include.lowest = TRUE,
              labels = c("<15%", "15–30%", "30–50%", "50–65%", "≥65%"))
calib <- d |>
  group_by(Band = band) |>
  summarise(Months = n(), `Mean predicted` = mean(prob), `Observed frequency` = mean(rec_next12), .groups = "drop")
calib |>
  gt() |> gt_atlas() |>
  fmt_percent(c(`Mean predicted`, `Observed frequency`), decimals = 0)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(callout("output", "How to read this",
  paste0("The model ranks well (AUC ", sprintf("%.2f", bt$auc), ") and is roughly calibrated: months it scores 50–65% were followed by a recession ",
         fmt_pct(calib$`Observed frequency`[calib$Band == "50–65%"], 0), " of the time. ",
         "It is <b>not</b> a sharp alarm. At a 50% threshold it flags only about ", fmt_pct(bt$hit_rate, 0),
         " of pre-recession months, and its peak in the 12 months before the ",
         paste(bt$episodes$recession[bt$episodes$runup_peak < 0.5], collapse = ", "),
         " recessions began stayed below 50%. ",
         "Read it as a risk gauge that rises early and gradually, not as a binary signal.")))
cat(callout("warn", "How much weight the backtest can bear",
  "Four recessions fall in the scored period, and adjacent months share 11 of 12 target months, so the effective sample is far smaller than the month count. Differences of a few thousandths in Brier score between model variants are not statistically meaningful. The inputs are final-vintage FRED data (revised payrolls, seasonal factors, CPI), and the predictor set, the sign constraints and the 30-year window were chosen after looking at this history, so the backtest is optimistic relative to true real-time performance."))
```

# 8 — Refit cadence: why January, and what the alternatives would say

The model is refit once a year, in January. This section records the evidence behind keeping that schedule. Every variant uses the same data, predictors, scaler, constraints and CV rule; only *when* and *on what window* the model is fitted changes.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cadence
cm <- snap$cmp; lab <- snap$cmp_labels
cad <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(cm), function(k) {
  d <- cm[[k]]; dd <- d[!is.na(d$y) & !is.na(d$prob), ]
  n1 <- sum(dd$y == 1); n0 <- sum(dd$y == 0)
  data.frame(
    Option = k, Description = lab[[k]],
    Now = d$prob[d$date == latest],
    Brier = mean((dd$prob - dd$y)^2),
    AUC = (sum(rank(dd$prob)[dd$y == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0),
    FA = mean(dd$prob[dd$y == 0] > 0.5)
  )
}))
cad |>
  gt() |> gt_atlas() |>
  fmt_percent(c(Now, FA), decimals = 1) |>
  fmt_number(c(Brier, AUC), decimals = 3) |>
  cols_label(Now = paste("Probability,", fmt_mon(latest)), FA = "False alarms at 50%") |>
  tab_style(cell_fill("#fff3e6"), cells_body(rows = Option == "A")) |>
  tab_style(cell_text(weight = "bold"), cells_body(rows = Option == "A"))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
jmp <- abs(snap$jumps$jump)
lag_total <- length(seq(m$train_end, latest, by = "month")) - 1L
cat(callout("logic", "Findings",
  paste0(
  "<ul style='margin:0;padding-left:1.1rem;'>",
  "<li><b>The choice barely moves today's number.</b> Every rolling-window variant (A–C, F) puts the current probability between ",
  fmt_pct(min(cad$Now[cad$Option %in% c("A","B","C","F")]), 0), " and ", fmt_pct(max(cad$Now[cad$Option %in% c("A","B","C","F")]), 0), ".</li>",
  "<li><b>Refitting more often is not meaningfully better.</b> Monthly vs annual changes Brier by ", sprintf("%.4f", cad$Brier[cad$Option == "A"] - cad$Brier[cad$Option == "C"]), ", well inside the noise of four recessions.</li>",
  "<li><b>An expanding window is worse</b> (D, E): 1960s–70s relationships dilute the model and double the yield-curve coefficient, raising false alarms.</li>",
  "<li><b>Never refitting is worse still</b> (G): a model frozen in 1985 reads ", fmt_pct(cad$Now[cad$Option == "G"], 0), " today and has a ", fmt_pct(cad$FA[cad$Option == "G"], 0), " false-alarm rate.</li>",
  "<li><b>The cost of the annual cadence is a step each January</b>: scoring the same January with the new rather than the old model moves the probability by a mean of ", sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(jmp)), " pp (maximum ", sprintf("%.1f", 100 * max(jmp)), " pp, in ", snap$jumps$year[which.max(jmp)], "; the last eight refits were all within ±", sprintf("%.1f", 100 * max(abs(tail(snap$jumps$jump, 8)))), " pp).</li>",
  "<li>The live model is also stale between refits: its labels stop in ", fmt_mon(m$train_end), ", ", lag_total, " months before the month it scores. Twelve of those months are the embargo that any schedule has; the other ", lag_total - 12, " are the cost of waiting for January.</li></ul>")))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-betapath
#| fig-cap: "Coefficient on each predictor in every January model since 1985. Signs and rough sizes are stable, but the slopes drift: in recent Januaries baa_spread has risen, claims_rise has fallen and the yield-curve slope has weakened (about −1.2 to −0.6 over the last two refits). That drift is the source of the January step."
snap$beta_path |>
  filter(term != "intercept") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, beta)) +
  geom_step(color = NAVY, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = GREY, linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~term, scales = "free_y", nrow = 3) +

```

# 9 — How the output is used downstream

- **Growth-outlook card.** Shows the probability, tier and the nine $\beta_jz_j$ contributions (the bar chart in section 6.1), plus a link to the published recession tracker, which uses the same method.
- **GDP forecast.** A regression maps a separate composite macro score to next-quarter real GDP growth. The recession probability (using the backtest's out-of-sample series, so there is no look-ahead) is added to that regression **only if** its coefficient is negative and significant ($t<-1.96$); if so, $\text{GDP}=a+b\cdot\text{score}+c\cdot p_{\text{rec}}$ and the drag is shown on the card. Otherwise it plays no part in the forecast.
- **LLM context.** The probability, tier and top drivers are passed to the LLM insight prompts (`R/llm_insights.R`).
- **Caching.** Fetch, fit and backtest run together in `train_recession_glm()`; the result is cached in memory for one day.

# 10 — Limitations and risks

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(callout("warn", "Statistical",
  paste0(
  "<ul style='margin:0;padding-left:1.1rem;'>",
  "<li><b>Few events.</b> A handful of recessions (four since 1985) underlie every estimate. Coefficients and backtest metrics carry wide uncertainty that the app does not display; the probability is a point estimate with no interval.</li>",
  "<li><b>Overlapping labels.</b> Adjacent months share 11 of their 12 target months, so observations are heavily autocorrelated. The stratified random CV folds ignore this and are optimistic about out-of-sample error, which may lead the chosen penalty to be too weak.</li>",
  "<li><b>Selection after the fact.</b> The predictor set, sign constraints and window length were chosen with knowledge of the history they are then tested on.</li>",
  "<li><b>Constraints can hide a missing signal.</b> Prime-age LFPR is currently held at exactly 0 and ", names(which.min(abs(m$beta[m$beta != 0])))[1], " is close to it; with the sign constraint a predictor whose historical relationship has reversed simply drops out rather than flagging the change.</li></ul>")))
cat(callout("warn", "Data",
  paste0(
  "<ul style='margin:0;padding-left:1.1rem;'>",
  "<li><b>Final vintages.</b> Payrolls, unemployment, CPI and sentiment are revised after release; the backtest uses today's values, not what a forecaster saw.</li>",
  "<li><b>NBER dating lag.</b> The label for recent months is unknown and appears as 0 until the NBER dates a peak (section 3).</li>",
  "<li><b>Publication calendar.</b> Daily yields and weekly claims run a month ahead of the monthly macro series, so the latest scored month (", fmt_mon(latest), ") is the last month where every predictor exists; the newest yield and claims readings are not used until the monthly series catch up. A single missing month (for example during a government shutdown) is bridged by interpolation, longer gaps block scoring.</li>",
  "<li><b>Regime change.</b> The model learns from 30 years of relationships; a recession with a new cause (a pandemic, a non-monetary shock) is detected only through the labor and credit indicators it moves.</li></ul>")))
cat(callout("note", "Operational",
  "<ul style='margin:0;padding-left:1.1rem;'><li>The annual refit means the live model lags new data by up to 12 months of labels (section 8).</li><li>Any failure in fetching or fitting returns no model (<code>train_recession_glm()</code> returns <code>NULL</code>); since the hand-tuned fallback was removed there is no substitute estimate.</li><li>The 360-month window and 12-month embargo are constants in <code>R/synopsis_tier3.R</code>; changing them changes both the live reading and the backtest. The recession tracker must be kept on the same settings.</li></ul>"))
```

# 11 — Code map and reproduction

| Step | Function (`R/synopsis_tier3.R`) |
|---|---|
| Fetch the 13 series from 1959 | `.fetch_glm_series()` |
| Single-month gap fill | `.fill_single_gaps()` |
| Monthly panel, target and predictors | `build_glm_panel()` |
| Select training rows (window + embargo) | `.glm_training_rows()` |
| Median/MAD scaler and transform | `build_robust_scaler()`, `apply_robust_scaler()` |
| Fixed, stratified CV folds | `.cv_folds()` |
| Sign limits for glmnet | `.glm_sign_limits()` |
| Fit (Ridge, constrained, λ₁ₛₑ) | `fit_recession_glm()` |
| Score | `predict_recession_glm()` |
| Walk-forward backtest and metrics | `backtest_recession_glm()` |
| Fit + score latest + backtest, one call | `train_recession_glm()` |
| Card payload (β·z, tier) | `.compute_recession_prob()`, `.classify_recession_tier()` |

To regenerate this document with fresh data: run `Rscript docs/build_recession_snapshot.R`, then `quarto render docs/recession_model.qmd`. The snapshot was built `r format(snap$built_at, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")` and scores **`r fmt_mon(latest)`**.

<details>
<summary>Glossary</summary>

**Base rate (climatology)**
: Share of months in the training window with $y=1$. A model that always predicts this number is the "no-skill" benchmark.

**Brier score**
: Mean squared error of a probability forecast against the 0/1 outcome; lower is better, 0 is perfect.

**Clamp**
: Cap a value to a range; here $z$ is limited to $[-3,3]$.

**Cross-validation (CV)**
: Splitting the training data into folds, fitting on all but one and scoring on the one held out, to choose $\lambda$ without using the test data.

**Deviance (binomial)**
: $-2\times$ the average log-likelihood of the labels; the loss that logistic regression minimises.

**Embargo**
: The 12-month gap between the as-of date and the latest training row, so that no label overlaps the future.

**λ (lambda)**
: Strength of the Ridge penalty. Larger $\lambda$ means smaller, more stable coefficients.

**λ₁ₛₑ ("one-standard-error rule")**
: The largest $\lambda$ whose CV error is within one standard error of the best; favours the simpler, more shrunk model.

**Log-odds (logit)**
: $\log\frac{p}{1-p}$. The model is linear on this scale; $\sigma$ converts it back to a probability.

**MAD**
: Median absolute deviation, scaled by 1.4826; a robust analogue of the standard deviation.

**NBER**
: The National Bureau of Economic Research committee that dates US business-cycle peaks and troughs; the source of `USREC`.

**Pseudo-out-of-sample**
: Scored only with information available at the time, but using today's data vintages and today's design choices.

**Ridge (α = 0)**
: Regularisation that penalises the sum of squared coefficients.

**Sign constraint**
: A bound that forces a coefficient to be $\ge 0$ or $\le 0$, according to macro theory.

**Walk-forward**
: Re-fitting the model at each step through time and scoring only the period after the fit.

</details>
